question.full_text:
At what temperature will the rms speed of oxygen molecules become just sufficient for escaping from the Earth's atmosphere? (Given : Mass of oxygen molecule $(m) = 2.76 \times 10^{-26}\,\mathrm{kg}$ Boltzmann's constant $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{JK^{-1}}$)
(1) $2.508 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$
(2) $5.016 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$
(3) $8.360 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$
(4) $1.254 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$
question.html:
At what temperature will the rms speed of oxygen molecules become just sufficient for escaping from the Earth's atmosphere? (Given : Mass of oxygen molecule (m) = 2.76 × 10-26 kg Boltzmann's constant kB = 1.38 × 10-23 JK-1)
  1. (1)2.508 × 104 K
  2. (2)5.016 × 104 K
  3. (3)8.360 × 104 K
  4. (4)1.254 × 104 K
question.stem: At what temperature will the rms speed of oxygen molecules become just sufficient for escaping from the Earth's atmosphere? (Given : Mass of oxygen molecule $(m) = 2.76 \times 10^{-26}\,\mathrm{kg}$ Boltzmann's constant $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{JK^{-1}}$)

solution.full_text:
1. $V_{\mathrm{escape}} = 11200\,\mathrm{m/s}$
2. Say at temperature $T$ it attains $V_{\mathrm{escape}}$
3. So, $\sqrt{\frac{3k_{B}T}{m_{\mathrm{O_2}}}} = 11200\,\mathrm{m/s}$
4. On solving,
5. $T = 8.360 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$
solution.html:
1. Vescape = 11200 m/s
  2. Say at temperature T it attains Vescape
  3. So, 3kBTmO2 = 11200 m/s
  4. On solving,
  5. T = 8.360 × 104 K
steps: $V_{\mathrm{escape}} = 11200\,\mathrm{m/s}$
Say at temperature $T$ it attains $V_{\mathrm{escape}}$
So, $\sqrt{\frac{3k_{B}T}{m_{\mathrm{O_2}}}} = 11200\,\mathrm{m/s}$
On solving,
printed_lines: Say at temperature T it attains V_{escape}

steps: Escape requires $v_{rms} = v_e$, with Earth's escape speed $v_e = 11.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} = 1.12 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
$v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3 k_B T}{m}}$, so $T = \frac{m v_e^{2}}{3 k_B}$.
$T = \frac{2}{3} \times 10^{-3} \times 1.2544 \times 10^{8} = 8.363 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K} \approx 8.360 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Escape requires vrms = ve, with Earth's escape speed ve = 11.2 km s-1 = 1.12 × 104 m s-1.
  2. vrms = 3 kB Tm, so T = m ve23 kB.
  3. m3 kB = 2.76 × 10-263 × 1.38 × 10-23 = 23 × 10-3 K s2 m-2.
  4. ve2 = (1.12 × 104)2 = 1.2544 × 108 m2 s-2.
  5. T = 23 × 10-3 × 1.2544 × 108 = 8.363 × 104 K ≈ 8.360 × 104 K, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Set v_rms = sqrt(3kT/m) equal to Earth's escape speed 11.2 km/s, giving T = m v^2/(3k) = 8.36 x 10^4 K.

question.full_text:
The volume (V) of a monatomic gas varies with its temperature (T), as shown in the graph. The ratio of work done by the gas, to the heat absorbed by it, when it undergoes a change from state A to state B, is
[Figure: V-T graph: straight line through origin O, process A to B along it]
(1) $\frac{2}{5}$
(2) $\frac{1}{3}$
(3) $\frac{2}{3}$
(4) $\frac{2}{7}$
question.html:
The volume (V) of a monatomic gas varies with its temperature (T), as shown in the graph. The ratio of work done by the gas, to the heat absorbed by it, when it undergoes a change from state A to state B, is
  1. (1)25
  2. (2)13
  3. (3)23
  4. (4)27
question.stem: The volume (V) of a monatomic gas varies with its temperature (T), as shown in the graph. The ratio of work done by the gas, to the heat absorbed by it, when it undergoes a change from state A to state B, is

figures.text: V-T graph: straight line through origin O, process A to B along it

checks.print_match: all 5 label(s) printed; 100% of the spec's lines on the printed ones, 78% of the printed lines covered

spec.title: V-T graph: straight line through origin O, process A to B along it

solution.full_text:
1. Given process is isobaric
2. $dQ = n\,C_p\,dT$
3. $dQ = n\left(\frac{5}{2}R\right)dT$
4. $dW = P\,dV = n\,R\,dT$
5. Required ratio $= \frac{dW}{dQ} = \frac{nRdT}{n\left(\frac{5}{2}R\right)dT} = \frac{2}{5}$
solution.html:
1. Given process is isobaric
  2. dQ = n Cp dT
  3. dQ = n(52R)dT
  4. dW = P dV = n R dT
  5. Required ratio = dWdQ = nRdTn(52R)dT = 25
steps: Given process is isobaric
$dQ = n\,C_p\,dT$
$dQ = n\left(\frac{5}{2}R\right)dT$
$dW = P\,dV = n\,R\,dT$
Required ratio $= \frac{dW}{dQ} = \frac{nRdT}{n\left(\frac{5}{2}R\right)dT} = \frac{2}{5}$
The graph is a straight line through the origin, so $V \propto T$, which means the pressure is constant (isobaric process).
Work done at constant pressure: $W = P\,\Delta V = nR\,\Delta T$.
Heat absorbed at constant pressure: $Q = nC_p\,\Delta T$, with $C_p = \frac{5}{2}R$ for a monatomic gas.
$\frac{W}{Q} = \frac{nR\,\Delta T}{n\cdot\frac{5}{2}R\,\Delta T} = \frac{2}{5}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The graph is a straight line through the origin, so V ∝ T, which means the pressure is constant (isobaric process).
  2. Work done at constant pressure: W = P Δ V = nR Δ T.
  3. Heat absorbed at constant pressure: Q = nCp Δ T, with Cp = 52R for a monatomic gas.
  4. WQ = nR Δ Tn·52R Δ T = 25, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: V-T graph is a straight line through the origin, so A to B is isobaric; W/Q = nR dT / (n Cp dT) = R/(5R/2) = 2/5.

question.full_text:
The efficiency of an ideal heat engine working between the freezing point and boiling point of water, is
(1) $26.8\%$
(2) $6.25\%$
(3) $20\%$
(4) $12.5\%$
question.html:
The efficiency of an ideal heat engine working between the freezing point and boiling point of water, is
  1. (1)26.8%
  2. (2)6.25%
  3. (3)20%
  4. (4)12.5%
question.stem: The efficiency of an ideal heat engine working between the freezing point and boiling point of water, is

solution.full_text:
1. Efficiency of ideal heat engine, $\eta = \left(1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)$
2. $T_2$ : Sink temperature
3. $T_1$ : Source temperature
4. $\%\eta = \left(1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) \times 100$
5. $= \left(1 - \frac{273}{373}\right) \times 100$
6. $= \left(\frac{100}{373}\right) \times 100 = 26.8\%$
solution.html:
1. Efficiency of ideal heat engine, η = (1 - T2T1)
  2. T2 : Sink temperature
  3. T1 : Source temperature
  4. %η = (1 - T2T1) × 100
  5. = (1 - 273373) × 100
  6. = (100373) × 100 = 26.8%
steps: Efficiency of ideal heat engine, $\eta = \left(1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)$
$T_2$ : Sink temperature
$T_1$ : Source temperature
$\%\eta = \left(1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) \times 100$
$= \left(1 - \frac{273}{373}\right) \times 100$
An ideal (Carnot) engine has $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$ with temperatures in kelvin.
Source at boiling point: $T_1 = 100^\circ\text{C} = 373\,\text{K}$; sink at freezing point: $T_2 = 0^\circ\text{C} = 273\,\text{K}$.
$\frac{100}{373} \approx 0.268 = 26.8\%$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. An ideal (Carnot) engine has η = 1 - T2T1 with temperatures in kelvin.
  2. Source at boiling point: T1 = 100°C = 373 K; sink at freezing point: T2 = 0°C = 273 K.
  3. η = 1 - 273373 = 100373.
  4. 100373 ≈ 0.268 = 26.8%, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Carnot efficiency between 273 K and 373 K is 1 - 273/373 = 100/373, about 26.8%.

question.full_text:
The fundamental frequency in an open organ pipe is equal to the third harmonic of a closed organ pipe. If the length of the closed organ pipe is $20\,\mathrm{cm}$, the length of the open organ pipe is
(1) $13.2\,\mathrm{cm}$
(2) $12.5\,\mathrm{cm}$
(3) $8\,\mathrm{cm}$
(4) $16\,\mathrm{cm}$
question.html:
The fundamental frequency in an open organ pipe is equal to the third harmonic of a closed organ pipe. If the length of the closed organ pipe is 20 cm, the length of the open organ pipe is
  1. (1)13.2 cm
  2. (2)12.5 cm
  3. (3)8 cm
  4. (4)16 cm
question.stem: The fundamental frequency in an open organ pipe is equal to the third harmonic of a closed organ pipe. If the length of the closed organ pipe is $20\,\mathrm{cm}$, the length of the open organ pipe is

solution.full_text:
1. For closed organ pipe, third harmonic $= \frac{3v}{4l}$
2. For open organ pipe, fundamental frequency $= \frac{v}{2l'}$
3. Given, $\frac{3v}{4l} = \frac{v}{2l'}$
4. $\Rightarrow l' = \frac{4l}{3\times 2} = \frac{2l}{3}$
5. $= \frac{2\times 20}{3} = 13.33\,\mathrm{cm}$
solution.html:
1. For closed organ pipe, third harmonic = 3v4l
  2. For open organ pipe, fundamental frequency = v2l'
  3. Given, 3v4l = v2l'
  4. ⇒ l' = 4l3× 2 = 2l3
  5. = 2× 203 = 13.33 cm
steps: For closed organ pipe, third harmonic $= \frac{3v}{4l}$
For open organ pipe, fundamental frequency $= \frac{v}{2l'}$
Given, $\frac{3v}{4l} = \frac{v}{2l'}$
$\Rightarrow l' = \frac{4l}{3\times 2} = \frac{2l}{3}$
$= \frac{2\times 20}{3} = 13.33\,\mathrm{cm}$
printed_lines: For closed organ pipe, third harmonic
For open organ pipe, fundamental frequency

steps: Fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe of length $L_o$: $f_o = \frac{v}{2L_o}$.
Third harmonic of a closed organ pipe of length $L_c$: $f_3 = \frac{3v}{4L_c}$.
Set them equal: $\frac{v}{2L_o} = \frac{3v}{4L_c}$.
Solve for $L_o$: $L_o = \frac{4L_c}{6} = \frac{2L_c}{3}$.
Substitute $L_c = 20\,\mathrm{cm}$: $L_o = \frac{2 \times 20}{3} = 13.33\,\mathrm{cm}$.
The nearest option is $13.2\,\mathrm{cm}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe of length Lo: fo = v2Lo.
  2. Third harmonic of a closed organ pipe of length Lc: f3 = 3v4Lc.
  3. Set them equal: v2Lo = 3v4Lc.
  4. Solve for Lo: Lo = 4Lc6 = 2Lc3.
  5. Substitute Lc = 20 cm: Lo = 2 × 203 = 13.33 cm.
  6. The nearest option is 13.2 cm, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Open pipe fundamental v/(2L_o) equals closed pipe third harmonic 3v/(4L_c), so L_o = 2L_c/3 = 40/3 = 13.33 cm, closest to 13.2 cm.

steps.text: A closed pipe of length 20 cm has modes $v/80$, $3v/80$, $5v/80$.
The third of these is $5v/80$; equating the open pipe's fundamental, $v/2L_o = 5v/80$, gives $L_o = 8\,\mathrm{cm}$.
steps.fix: The third harmonic is 3 times the fundamental, $3v/4L$; $5v/4L$ is the fifth harmonic, which is the second overtone.

other_options.proof: Equating $v/2L_o$ to the $k$-th harmonic of the closed pipe gives $L_o = 40/k$ cm, so the reachable lengths are 13.3 ($k=3$), 8 ($k=5$) and 5.7 ($k=7$). 12.5 cm needs $k = 3.2$, which is not a mode of either pipe; swapping which pipe is 20 cm long gives 30 cm, also not 12.5.

16 cm needs $k = 2.5$ in $L_o = 40/k$, and even harmonics are absent from a closed pipe. 16 cm is $4L/5$, the wavelength of the closed pipe's fifth harmonic, i.e. a wavelength rather than a pipe length, and the stem asks for a length.

question.full_text:
An inductor $20\,\mathrm{mH}$, a capacitor $100\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ and a resistor $50\,\Omega$ are connected in series across a source of emf, $V = 10\sin 314\,t$. The power loss in the circuit is
(1) $0.79\,\mathrm{W}$
(2) $2.74\,\mathrm{W}$
(3) $0.43\,\mathrm{W}$
(4) $1.13\,\mathrm{W}$
question.html:
An inductor 20 mH, a capacitor 100 μF and a resistor 50 Ω are connected in series across a source of emf, V = 10sin 314 t. The power loss in the circuit is
  1. (1)0.79 W
  2. (2)2.74 W
  3. (3)0.43 W
  4. (4)1.13 W
question.stem: An inductor $20\,\mathrm{mH}$, a capacitor $100\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ and a resistor $50\,\Omega$ are connected in series across a source of emf, $V = 10\sin 314\,t$. The power loss in the circuit is

solution.full_text:
1. $P_{av} = \left(\frac{V_{RMS}}{Z}\right)^{2} R$
2. $Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + \left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}} = 56\,\Omega$
3. $\therefore\ P_{av} = \left(\frac{10}{\left(\sqrt{2}\right)56}\right)^{2} \times 50 = 0.79\,\mathrm{W}$
solution.html:
1. Pav = (VRMSZ)2 R
  2. Z = R2 + (ω L - 1ω C)2 = 56 Ω
  3. ∴ Pav = (10(2)56)2 × 50 = 0.79 W
steps: $P_{av} = \left(\frac{V_{RMS}}{Z}\right)^{2} R$
$Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + \left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}} = 56\,\Omega$
$\therefore\ P_{av} = \left(\frac{10}{\left(\sqrt{2}\right)56}\right)^{2} \times 50 = 0.79\,\mathrm{W}$
From $V = 10\sin 314t$: $V_0 = 10\,\mathrm{V}$ and $\omega = 314\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
$X_L = \omega L = 314 \times 20\times10^{-3} = 6.28\,\Omega$.
$X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{314 \times 100\times10^{-6}} = 31.85\,\Omega$.
$V_{rms}^2 = \left(\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = 50\,\mathrm{V^2}$.
$P = I_{rms}^2 R = \frac{V_{rms}^2 R}{Z^2} = \frac{50 \times 50}{3153.8} \approx 0.79\,\mathrm{W}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. From V = 10sin 314t: V0 = 10 V and ω = 314 rad s-1.
  2. XL = ω L = 314 × 20×10-3 = 6.28 Ω.
  3. XC = 1ω C = 1314 × 100×10-6 = 31.85 Ω.
  4. XC - XL = 31.85 - 6.28 = 25.57 Ω.
  5. Z2 = R2 + (XC - XL)2 = 2500 + 653.8 = 3153.8 Ω2, so Z ≈ 56.16 Ω.
  6. Vrms2 = (102)2 = 50 V2.
  7. P = Irms2 R = Vrms2 RZ2 = 50 × 503153.8 ≈ 0.79 W, which is option 1.

step_list: Read omega = 314 rad/s and peak V0 = 10 V from V = 10 sin 314t
Inductive reactance X_L = omega*L = 314 x 0.02 = 6.28 ohm
Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(omega*C) = 1/(314 x 1e-4) ~ 31.8 ohm
Impedance Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2) = sqrt(2500 + 25.6^2) ~ 56 ohm
Convert to rms and compute average power P = I_rms^2 R = V0^2 R / (2 Z^2) (equivalently V_rms I_rms cos phi)
difficulty.why: Hard on both spines: five computational steps with no calculator (a reciprocal 1/0.0314, squaring 25.6, a square root of about 3150) and then a real rival one factor of sqrt(2) away, so a candidate who does all the long work correctly can still lose it on the last line's peak/rms conversion.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Long to execute rather than hard to plan: the method is the standard signposted series-LCR route, but the arithmetic (reciprocal for X_C, squaring the net reactance, square root for Z) is slow by hand, and the source gives a PEAK emf, so the rms conversion must be applied consistently to both V and I - doing it to only one lands exactly on the sqrt(2) rival.

trap.label: formula_misused
trap.route: Adding resistance and net reactance arithmetically, $Z = 50 + (31.85-6.28) = 75.57\,\Omega$, instead of in quadrature gives $P = V_{rms}^2R/Z^2 = 2500/5712 = 0.43\,\mathrm{W}$
trap.who: a student who computes both reactances correctly and then totals the three series elements the way series resistances are totalled
trap.feels: the elements are in series, and in every earlier circuit chapter series elements simply add

steps.text: With $\omega = 314$, $X_L = 6.28\,\Omega$ and $X_C = 31.85\,\Omega$, so the net reactance is $25.57\,\Omega$.
In series the elements add, so $Z = 50 + 25.57 = 75.57\,\Omega$ and $P = V_{rms}^2R/Z^2 = 0.43\,\mathrm{W}$.
steps.fix: Reactance is 90 degrees out of phase with resistance, so $Z = \sqrt{R^2+(X_C-X_L)^2} = 56.2\,\Omega$, giving 0.79 W.

other_options.proof: $P = V_{rms}^2R/Z^2 = 2500/Z^2$, and since $R = 50\,\Omega$ the impedance cannot fall below 50, so this expression cannot exceed 1 W; 2.74 W would need $Z = 30\,\Omega$. Using the peak voltage instead of the rms value doubles the key to 1.59 W, and $\sqrt{R^2-(X_C-X_L)^2} = 42.97\,\Omega$ with the peak voltage gives 2.71 W, not 2.74 W.

1.13 W needs $Z = 47\,\Omega$, again below $R$. The wrong-impedance routes available give 0.63 W (reactances added), 0.98 W ($X_C$ ignored), 0.71 W ($X_L$ ignored), 1.00 W ($Z$ taken as $R$), 0.89 W ($V_{rms}^2/Z$) and 1.59 W (peak voltage used); none of them is 1.13 W.

question.full_text:
Current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is $5\,\mathrm{div/mA}$ and its voltage sensitivity (angular deflection per unit voltage applied) is $20\,\mathrm{div/V}$. The resistance of the galvanometer is
(1) $40\,\Omega$
(2) $250\,\Omega$
(3) $25\,\Omega$
(4) $500\,\Omega$
question.html:
Current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is 5 div/mA and its voltage sensitivity (angular deflection per unit voltage applied) is 20 div/V. The resistance of the galvanometer is
  1. (1)40 Ω
  2. (2)250 Ω
  3. (3)25 Ω
  4. (4)500 Ω
question.stem: Current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is $5\,\mathrm{div/mA}$ and its voltage sensitivity (angular deflection per unit voltage applied) is $20\,\mathrm{div/V}$. The resistance of the galvanometer is

solution.full_text:
1. Current sensitivity $I_S = \frac{NBA}{C}$
2. Voltage sensitivity $V_S = \frac{NBA}{CR_G}$
3. So, resistance of galvanometer $R_G = \frac{I_S}{V_S} = \frac{5 \times 1}{20 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{5000}{20} = 250\,\Omega$
solution.html:
1. Current sensitivity IS = NBAC
  2. Voltage sensitivity VS = NBACRG
  3. So, resistance of galvanometer RG = ISVS = 5 × 120 × 10-3 = 500020 = 250 Ω
steps: Current sensitivity $I_S = \frac{NBA}{C}$
Voltage sensitivity $V_S = \frac{NBA}{CR_G}$
So, resistance of galvanometer $R_G = \frac{I_S}{V_S} = \frac{5 \times 1}{20 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{5000}{20} = 250\,\Omega$
Voltage sensitivity is current sensitivity divided by resistance: $V_s = \frac{\theta}{V} = \frac{\theta}{IR} = \frac{I_s}{R}$.
Convert current sensitivity to SI: $I_s = 5\,\mathrm{div/mA} = 5000\,\mathrm{div/A}$.
$R = \frac{I_s}{V_s} = \frac{5000\,\mathrm{div/A}}{20\,\mathrm{div/V}} = 250\,\Omega$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Voltage sensitivity is current sensitivity divided by resistance: Vs = θV = θIR = IsR.
  2. Convert current sensitivity to SI: Is = 5 div/mA = 5000 div/A.
  3. R = IsVs = 5000 div/A20 div/V = 250 Ω, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Voltage sensitivity = current sensitivity / R, so R = (5000 div/A)/(20 div/V) = 250 ohm.

question.full_text:
A thin diamagnetic rod is placed vertically between the poles of an electromagnet. When the current in the electromagnet is switched on, then the diamagnetic rod is pushed up, out of the horizontal magnetic field. Hence the rod gains gravitational potential energy. The work required to do this comes from
(1) The current source
(2) The lattice structure of the material of the rod
(3) The magnetic field
(4) The induced electric field due to the changing magnetic field

  1. (1)The current source

question.stem: A thin diamagnetic rod is placed vertically between the poles of an electromagnet. When the current in the electromagnet is switched on, then the diamagnetic rod is pushed up, out of the horizontal magnetic field. Hence the rod gains gravitational potential energy. The work required to do this comes from

options.text: The lattice structure of the material of the rod
The induced electric field due to the changing magnetic field

solution.full_text: 1. Energy of current source will be converted into potential energy of the rod.
solution.html: 1. Energy of current source will be converted into potential energy of the rod.
steps: Energy of current source will be converted into potential energy of the rod.
printed_lines: Energy of current source will be converted
into potential energy of the rod.

steps: A diamagnetic rod is repelled from the strong-field region, so it is pushed up and gains gravitational potential energy $\Delta U = mgh$.
A magnetic field does no work on charges, since $\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, so the field is only the agent that transfers energy, not its source.

The energy stored in and transferred through the field comes from the current source that establishes and maintains the current in the electromagnet, so the work comes from the current source, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A diamagnetic rod is repelled from the strong-field region, so it is pushed up and gains gravitational potential energy Δ U = mgh.
  2. A magnetic field does no work on charges, since →F = q→v × →B is perpendicular to →v, so the field is only the agent that transfers energy, not its source.
  3. The energy stored in and transferred through the field comes from the current source that establishes and maintains the current in the electromagnet, so the work comes from the current source, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Static magnetic fields do no work; the energy to push the diamagnetic rod up is ultimately supplied by the current source that drives the electromagnet.

step_list: Apply energy conservation: the rod's gain in gravitational PE must be paid for by some energy source, so ask which option is a source rather than an agent

Recall that a magnetic field (magnetic force) does no work by itself -- the field only transmits/stores energy and is not the ultimate supplier, and the transient induced electric field exists only while the current is being switched on

solution.full_text:

steps: Heating increases thermal generation of electron-hole pairs, so the intrinsic carrier concentration $n_i$ rises.
Higher $n_i$ raises the minority-carrier reverse saturation current $I_0$, so the reverse resistance falls.
Higher temperature also lowers the barrier (knee) voltage, so the forward current at a given $V$ rises and the forward resistance falls.
Since both forward and reverse behaviour change, the overall $V$-$I$ characteristic is affected, which is option $4$.

  2. Higher ni raises the minority-carrier reverse saturation current I0, so the reverse resistance falls.
  3. Higher temperature also lowers the barrier (knee) voltage, so the forward current at a given V rises and the forward resistance falls.
  4. Since both forward and reverse behaviour change, the overall V-I characteristic is affected, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Heating raises intrinsic carrier concentration, increasing reverse saturation current and lowering the forward knee voltage, so both forward and reverse behaviour change: the whole V-I characteristic is affected.

subtopics.name: VI Characteristics of PN Junction Diode
subtopics.why: The answer is that heating a p-n junction changes both its forward and reverse behaviour, so it affects the overall V-I characteristics of the diode.

step_list: Recall that heating thermally generates more electron-hole pairs, so carrier concentration (minority carriers especially) rises in the junction material
Apply it to reverse bias: the reverse saturation current is carried by minority carriers and rises with temperature, so reverse conduction changes (rules out options 2 and 3)

Apply it to forward bias: more carriers and a lower barrier/knee voltage give more forward current at the same voltage, so forward conduction changes too (rules out option 1); both regions change, so the whole V-I curve shifts
difficulty.why: Three short conceptual steps: one mechanism (thermal generation of carriers) checked against both bias regions, and option 1 is what you get if you check only the reverse region, so only the forward-bias check separates it from option 4.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The word 'only' in options 1 and 3: a careless candidate goes from the familiar fact that reverse saturation current rises with temperature to option 1 without checking forward bias. NCERT never prints a line on how temperature affects a diode, so this has to be reasoned from intrinsic carrier generation, not recalled.

source.note: Image matches text layer draft. 'not' appears in lower case only inside option (2) ('Does not affect...'); the stem itself is not negatively phrased. No figure, no footer text.

categories.concept: Heating a p-n junction shifts both branches of its characteristic: the reverse saturation current rises and the barrier potential falls

trap.label: half_right
trap.route: The temperature fact that is actually stored is about the reverse branch, that the reverse saturation current roughly doubles for every ten degrees, so 'affects only reverse resistance' is a true half of the story with the word 'only' accepted along with it
trap.who: a student who has learnt the temperature dependence of the reverse saturation current and has not been asked about the forward branch
trap.feels: the reverse branch is the one the chapter discusses temperature with, so limiting the effect to it looks like the precise answer rather than the partial one

steps.text: Heating does raise the reverse saturation current, so the reverse resistance changes.
Therefore it affects only the reverse resistance.
steps.fix: The barrier potential falls with temperature too, so the knee of the forward branch moves; the whole V-I characteristic shifts.

other_options.who: a student working from the general rule that a semiconductor's conductivity rises with temperature
other_options.feels: the forward branch is the conducting branch, so a rule about conduction seems to belong there and nowhere else

steps.text: Heating generates more carriers, so the diode conducts more readily in forward bias.
So heating affects only the forward resistance.
steps.fix: The same extra carriers raise the reverse saturation current, which is the more temperature-sensitive of the two branches.

other_options.proof: Both printed temperature facts of the chapter point the other way: the reverse saturation current is strongly temperature dependent and the barrier potential decreases with temperature. Checked whether any route from 'the resistance of a semiconductor decreases with temperature' can arrive at no effect at all, and it cannot, since that rule itself asserts a change.

solution.full_text:
1. When reflected light rays and refracted rays are perpendicular, reflected light is polarised with electric field vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
[Figure: Unpolarised light incident at angle i on a surface of index mu: reflected ray (dots only) perpendicular to refracted ray]
2. Also, $\tan i = \mu$ (Brewster angle)

steps: Reflected and refracted rays perpendicular gives $i + r = 90^\circ$, so $r = 90^\circ - i$.
Snell's law: $\sin i = \mu \sin r = \mu \sin(90^\circ - i) = \mu \cos i$.
Hence $\tan i = \mu$, i.e. $i = \tan^{-1}\mu$ (Brewster's law), so options $2$ ($i = \sin^{-1}(1/\mu)$) and $4$ ($i = \tan^{-1}(1/\mu)$) are wrong.

At the Brewster angle the component of $\vec{E}$ parallel to the plane of incidence is not reflected, so the reflected light is plane polarised with $\vec{E}$ perpendicular to the plane of incidence, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Reflected and refracted rays perpendicular gives i + r = 90°, so r = 90° - i.
  2. Snell's law: sin i = μ sin r = μ sin(90° - i) = μ cos i.
  3. Hence tan i = μ, i.e. i = tan-1μ (Brewster's law), so options 2 (i = sin-1(1/μ)) and 4 (i = tan-1(1/μ)) are wrong.
  4. At the Brewster angle the component of →E parallel to the plane of incidence is not reflected, so the reflected light is plane polarised with →E perpendicular to the plane of incidence, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Reflected and refracted rays perpendicular means i is the Brewster angle (tan i = mu), and the reflected light is then fully polarised with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence.

step_list: Read 'reflected and refracted rays perpendicular to each other' as the Brewster (polarising-angle) condition: r = 90 deg - i.
Put r = 90 deg - i into Snell's law (sin i = mu sin r = mu cos i) to get Brewster's law tan i = mu, and check the two angle options 2 and 4 against it.
Recall which component of the electric vector survives reflection at Brewster incidence (the in-plane component is not reflected) to decide between the two polarisation statements, options 1 and 3.
difficulty.why: Hard: short recalls, but the question joins two separate facts (the Brewster angle and the polarisation direction of the reflected beam) and plants a trap on each, a one-word parallel/perpendicular swap between 1 and 3 and an inverted tan i = 1/mu in 4, so three options stay in play and only both pieces of knowledge, held the right way round, separate them.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Two traps, one per concept: 1 vs 3 is the altered-word rival (parallel vs perpendicular to the plane of incidence), where a candidate who pictures the reflected E as 'lying in the plane' picks the wrong one; 4 is the inverted Brewster relation reached by a careless Snell's-law setup. Option 2 is a decoy from total internal reflection and is dismissed on sight.

question.full_text:
In Young's double slit experiment the separation $d$ between the slits is $2\,\mathrm{mm}$, the wavelength $\lambda$ of the light used is $5896\,\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ and distance $D$ between the screen and slits is $100\,\mathrm{cm}$. It is found that the angular width of the fringes is $0.20^\circ$. To increase the fringe angular width to $0.21^\circ$ (with same $\lambda$ and $D$) the separation between the slits needs to be changed to
(1) $1.8\,\mathrm{mm}$
(2) $2.1\,\mathrm{mm}$
(3) $1.9\,\mathrm{mm}$
(4) $1.7\,\mathrm{mm}$
question.html:
In Young's double slit experiment the separation d between the slits is 2 mm, the wavelength λ of the light used is 5896 ˚A and distance D between the screen and slits is 100 cm. It is found that the angular width of the fringes is 0.20°. To increase the fringe angular width to 0.21° (with same λ and D) the separation between the slits needs to be changed to
  1. (1)1.8 mm
  2. (2)2.1 mm
  3. (3)1.9 mm
  4. (4)1.7 mm
question.stem: In Young's double slit experiment the separation $d$ between the slits is $2\,\mathrm{mm}$, the wavelength $\lambda$ of the light used is $5896\,\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ and distance $D$ between the screen and slits is $100\,\mathrm{cm}$. It is found that the angular width of the fringes is $0.20^\circ$. To increase the fringe angular width to $0.21^\circ$ (with same $\lambda$ and $D$) the separation between the slits needs to be changed to

solution.full_text:
1. Angular width $= \frac{\lambda}{d}$
2. $0.20^\circ = \frac{\lambda}{2\,\mathrm{mm}}$ ...(i)
3. $0.21^\circ = \frac{\lambda}{d}$ ...(ii)
4. Dividing we get, $\frac{0.20}{0.21} = \frac{d}{2\,\mathrm{mm}}$
5. $\therefore\ d = 1.9\,\mathrm{mm}$
solution.html:
1. Angular width = λd
  2. 0.20° = λ2 mm ...(i)
  3. 0.21° = λd ...(ii)
  4. Dividing we get, 0.200.21 = d2 mm
  5. ∴ d = 1.9 mm
steps: Angular width $= \frac{\lambda}{d}$
$0.20^\circ = \frac{\lambda}{2\,\mathrm{mm}}$ ...(i)
$0.21^\circ = \frac{\lambda}{d}$ ...(ii)
Dividing we get, $\frac{0.20}{0.21} = \frac{d}{2\,\mathrm{mm}}$
$\therefore\ d = 1.9\,\mathrm{mm}$
Angular fringe width in YDSE: $\theta = \frac{\lambda}{d}$, independent of $D$.
With $\lambda$ fixed, $\theta d = \text{constant}$, so $d' = d\,\frac{\theta}{\theta'}$.
$d' = 2\,\mathrm{mm} \times \frac{0.20^\circ}{0.21^\circ} = 1.905\,\mathrm{mm} \approx 1.9\,\mathrm{mm}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Angular fringe width in YDSE: θ = λd, independent of D.
  2. With λ fixed, θ d = constant, so d' = d θθ'.
  3. d' = 2 mm × 0.20°0.21° = 1.905 mm ≈ 1.9 mm, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Angular fringe width theta = lambda/d, so d is inversely proportional to theta: d' = 2 mm x 0.20/0.21 = 1.905 mm, about 1.9 mm.

Options 1 and 4 drop away once the ratio is formed, and 20/21 is easy enough to work out that the arithmetic does not separate 1.9 from 1.8 or 1.7.

To raise $\theta$ from 0.20 to 0.21, scale $d$ by $0.21/0.20$: $d' = 2.1\,\mathrm{mm}$.
steps.fix: $\theta$ varies inversely with $d$, so $d' = d\,\theta/\theta' = 2\times20/21 = 1.9\,\mathrm{mm}$.

other_options.proof: The only ratio the data contain is 20:21, which gives $1.90\,\mathrm{mm}$ one way and $2.10\,\mathrm{mm}$ the other. 1.8 mm is a 10 per cent reduction of 2 mm, while the fractional change the stem supplies is $0.01/0.20 = 5$ per cent, which gives 1.90 mm; the only other arithmetic available, subtracting the printed degrees from the printed millimetres, mixes two unlike units.

1.7 mm is a 15 per cent reduction, and no 15 per cent step exists in the data. The values reachable from $d\,\theta/\theta'$ and $d\,\theta'/\theta$ are 1.90 and 2.10 mm, and bringing $\lambda$ or $D$ into the ratio is barred because the stem fixes both ('with same $\lambda$ and $D$').

(1) Small focal length and large diameter
(2) Large focal length and large diameter
(3) Large focal length and small diameter
(4) Small focal length and small diameter

answer.publisher_text: Large focal length and large diameter
answer.ai_text: Large focal length and large diameter

solution.full_text:
1. For telescope, angular magnification $= \frac{f_0}{f_E}$
2. So, focal length of objective lens should be large.
3. Angular resolution $= \frac{D}{1.22\lambda}$ should be large.
4. So, objective should have large focal length $(f_0)$ and large diameter $D$.
solution.html:
1. For telescope, angular magnification = f0fE
  2. So, focal length of objective lens should be large.
  3. Angular resolution = D1.22λ should be large.
  4. So, objective should have large focal length (f0) and large diameter D.
steps: For telescope, angular magnification $= \frac{f_0}{f_E}$
So, focal length of objective lens should be large.
Angular resolution $= \frac{D}{1.22\lambda}$ should be large.
So, objective should have large focal length $(f_0)$ and large diameter $D$.
printed_lines: So, focal length of objective lens should be
So, objective should have large focal length

steps: Angular magnification of an astronomical telescope is $m = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$, so a large objective focal length $f_o$ gives large magnification.
The limit of resolution is $\Delta\theta = \frac{1.22\,\lambda}{D}$, so resolving power $\frac{1}{\Delta\theta} = \frac{D}{1.22\,\lambda}$ increases with objective diameter $D$.
Both conditions need large focal length and large diameter, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Angular magnification of an astronomical telescope is m = fofe, so a large objective focal length fo gives large magnification.
  2. The limit of resolution is Δθ = 1.22 λD, so resolving power 1Δθ = D1.22 λ increases with objective diameter D.
  3. Both conditions need large focal length and large diameter, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Angular magnification m = f_o/f_e grows with objective focal length, and resolving power D/(1.22 lambda) grows with objective diameter, so both must be large.

question.full_text:
An electron of mass $m$ with an initial velocity $\vec{V} = V_0\hat{i}$ ($V_0 > 0$) enters an electric field $\vec{E} = -E_0\hat{i}$ ($E_0 = \text{constant} > 0$) at $t = 0$. If $\lambda_0$ is its de-Broglie wavelength initially, then its de-Broglie wavelength at time $t$ is
(1) $\dfrac{\lambda_0}{\left(1+\dfrac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right)}$
(2) $\lambda_0 t$
(3) $\lambda_0\left(1+\dfrac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right)$
(4) $\lambda_0$

An electron of mass m with an initial velocity →V = V0ˆı (V0 > 0) enters an electric field →E = -E0ˆı (E0 = constant > 0) at t = 0. If λ0 is its de-Broglie wavelength initially, then its de-Broglie wavelength at time t is

question.stem: An electron of mass $m$ with an initial velocity $\vec{V} = V_0\hat{i}$ ($V_0 > 0$) enters an electric field $\vec{E} = -E_0\hat{i}$ ($E_0 = \text{constant} > 0$) at $t = 0$. If $\lambda_0$ is its de-Broglie wavelength initially, then its de-Broglie wavelength at time $t$ is

solution.full_text:
1. Initial de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda_0 = \frac{h}{mV_0}$ ...(i)
[Figure: An electron between two field lines of E0 pointing left, with arrows F and V0]
2. Acceleration of electron $a = \frac{eE_0}{m}$
3. Velocity after time 't' $V = \left(V_0 + \frac{eE_0}{m}t\right)$
4. So, $\lambda = \frac{h}{mV} = \frac{h}{m\left(V_0 + \frac{eE_0}{m}t\right)}$
5. $= \frac{h}{mV_0\left[1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right]} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\left[1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right]}$ ...(ii)
6. Divide (ii) by (i), $\lambda = \frac{\lambda_0}{\left[1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right]}$
solution.html:
1. Initial de-Broglie wavelength λ0 = hmV0 ...(i)
  2. Acceleration of electron a = eE0m
  3. Velocity after time 't' V = (V0 + eE0mt)
  4. So, λ = hmV = hm(V0 + eE0mt)
  5. = hmV0[1 + eE0mV0t] = λ0[1 + eE0mV0t] ...(ii)
  6. Divide (ii) by (i), λ = λ0[1 + eE0mV0t]
steps: Initial de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda_0 = \frac{h}{mV_0}$ ...(i)
Acceleration of electron $a = \frac{eE_0}{m}$
Velocity after time 't' $V = \left(V_0 + \frac{eE_0}{m}t\right)$
So, $\lambda = \frac{h}{mV} = \frac{h}{m\left(V_0 + \frac{eE_0}{m}t\right)}$
$= \frac{h}{mV_0\left[1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right]} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\left[1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right]}$ ...(ii)
Divide (ii) by (i), $\lambda = \frac{\lambda_0}{\left[1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right]}$

spec.title: An electron between two field lines of E0 pointing left, with arrows F and V0

steps: Force on the electron: $\vec{F} = (-e)\vec{E} = (-e)(-E_0\hat{i}) = eE_0\hat{i}$, along $+\hat{i}$, the same direction as $\vec{V}$.
Acceleration: $a = \frac{eE_0}{m}$ along $+\hat{i}$, so the electron speeds up.
Velocity at time $t$: $v = V_0 + \frac{eE_0}{m}t = V_0\left(1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right)$.
Initial wavelength: $\lambda_0 = \frac{h}{mV_0}$.
Wavelength at time $t$: $\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{mV_0\left(1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right)} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\left(1 + \frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right)}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Force on the electron: →F = (-e)→E = (-e)(-E0ˆı) = eE0ˆı, along +ˆı, the same direction as →V.
  2. Acceleration: a = eE0m along +ˆı, so the electron speeds up.
  3. Velocity at time t: v = V0 + eE0mt = V0(1 + eE0mV0t).
  4. Initial wavelength: λ0 = hmV0.
  5. Wavelength at time t: λ = hmv = hmV0(1 + eE0mV0t) = λ0(1 + eE0mV0t), which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Force on electron F = -eE = +eE0 i, along its velocity, so v = V0 + (eE0/m)t and lambda = h/(mv) = lambda0/(1 + eE0 t/(m V0)).

question.full_text:
The ratio of kinetic energy to the total energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom, is
(1) $1 : 1$
(2) $2 : -1$
(3) $1 : -1$
(4) $1 : -2$
question.html:
The ratio of kinetic energy to the total energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom, is
  1. (1)1 : 1
  2. (2)2 : -1
  3. (3)1 : -1
  4. (4)1 : -2
question.stem: The ratio of kinetic energy to the total energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom, is

solution.full_text:
1. $\mathrm{KE} = -(\text{total energy})$
2. So, Kinetic energy : total energy $= 1 : -1$
solution.html:
1. KE = -(total energy)
  2. So, Kinetic energy : total energy = 1 : -1
steps: $\mathrm{KE} = -(\text{total energy})$
So, Kinetic energy : total energy $= 1 : -1$
Centripetal force from Coulomb attraction: $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{ke^2}{r^2}$, so $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{ke^2}{2r}$.
Potential energy: $U = -\frac{ke^2}{r}$.
Total energy: $E = K + U = \frac{ke^2}{2r} - \frac{ke^2}{r} = -\frac{ke^2}{2r} = -K$.
$K : E = K : (-K) = 1 : -1$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Centripetal force from Coulomb attraction: mv2r = ke2r2, so K = 12mv2 = ke22r.
  2. Potential energy: U = -ke2r.
  3. Total energy: E = K + U = ke22r - ke2r = -ke22r = -K.
  4. K : E = K : (-K) = 1 : -1, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: In a Bohr orbit KE = -E (total energy is negative and equal in magnitude to KE), so KE : E = 1 : -1.

question.full_text:
A set of '$n$' equal resistors, of value '$R$' each, are connected in series to a battery of emf '$E$' and internal resistance '$R$'. The current drawn is $I$. Now, the '$n$' resistors are connected in parallel to the same battery. Then the current drawn from battery becomes $10\,I$. The value of '$n$' is
(1) 10
(2) 20
(3) 11
(4) 9
question.html:
A set of 'n' equal resistors, of value 'R' each, are connected in series to a battery of emf 'E' and internal resistance 'R'. The current drawn is I. Now, the 'n' resistors are connected in parallel to the same battery. Then the current drawn from battery becomes 10 I. The value of 'n' is
  1. (1)10
  2. (2)20
  3. (3)11
  4. (4)9
question.stem: A set of '$n$' equal resistors, of value '$R$' each, are connected in series to a battery of emf '$E$' and internal resistance '$R$'. The current drawn is $I$. Now, the '$n$' resistors are connected in parallel to the same battery. Then the current drawn from battery becomes $10\,I$. The value of '$n$' is

solution.full_text:
1. $I = \frac{E}{nR + R}$ ...(i)
2. $10\,I = \frac{E}{\frac{R}{n} + R}$ ...(ii)
3. Dividing (ii) by (i),
4. $10 = \frac{(n + 1)R}{\left(\frac{1}{n} + 1\right)R}$
5. After solving the equation, $n = 10$
solution.html:
1. I = EnR + R ...(i)
  2. 10 I = ERn + R ...(ii)
  3. Dividing (ii) by (i),
  4. 10 = (n + 1)R(1n + 1)R
  5. After solving the equation, n = 10
steps: $I = \frac{E}{nR + R}$ ...(i)
Dividing (ii) by (i),
$10 = \frac{(n + 1)R}{\left(\frac{1}{n} + 1\right)R}$
After solving the equation, $n = 10$
In series, total resistance is $nR + R = (n+1)R$, so $I = \frac{E}{(n+1)R}$.
In parallel, the $n$ resistors give $\frac{R}{n}$, so total resistance is $\frac{R}{n} + R = \frac{(n+1)R}{n}$.
$I' = \frac{E}{(n+1)R/n} = \frac{nE}{(n+1)R} = nI$.
$I' = 10I \Rightarrow nI = 10I \Rightarrow n = 10$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In series, total resistance is nR + R = (n+1)R, so I = E(n+1)R.
  2. In parallel, the n resistors give Rn, so total resistance is Rn + R = (n+1)Rn.
  3. I' = E(n+1)R/n = nE(n+1)R = nI.
  4. I' = 10I ⇒ nI = 10I ⇒ n = 10, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Series: I = E/((n+1)R); parallel: I' = E/(R/n + R) = nE/((n+1)R) = nI, so 10I = nI gives n = 10.

trap.label: formula_misused
trap.route: Keeping the internal resistance in the parallel circuit but writing the series current as $E/(nR)$ leaves the ratio $n^2/(n+1)$, whose root for a tenfold rise is $10.9$, and 11 is the integer sitting in the options.

ways.name: the internal resistance dropped on the series side

steps.text: In parallel the total is $R/n + R = R(n+1)/n$, so $I' = nE/(R(n+1))$.
In series the total is just $nR$, so $I = E/(nR)$ and $I'/I = n^2/(n+1) = 10$, which gives $n \approx 10.9$, so 11.
steps.fix: The same internal resistance R is in the circuit both times: the series total is $(n+1)R$, and then the ratio is exactly n.

ways.name: 'becomes 10 I' read as a rise of 10 I

steps.text: Both currents share the factor $1/((n+1)R)$, so $I'/I = n$.
Take 'becomes $10\,I$' as $10\,I$ added on top of the original I, so $I' = 11I$ and $n = 11$.
steps.fix: The stem says the current becomes $10\,I$, so the new current is the ratio, not the increase.

other_options.proof: 20 is the root of $n/2 = 10$, and I looked for a halved ratio: dropping the internal resistance from the series side gives $n^2/(n+1)$, from the parallel side $n(n+1)$, from both $n^2$, and putting the internal resistance in parallel with the n resistors gives $(n+1)^2$. None of these has 20 as its root, and the exact ratio $I'/I = n$ cannot be halved by any single dropped or added term, so 20 is twice the key and nothing more.

9 is the root of $n+1 = 10$, so I checked whether any assembly of the stem's parts yields a ratio of $n+1$: the series total is $(n+1)R$ and the parallel total $R(n+1)/n$, and the $(n+1)$ cancels in the quotient, leaving n. The three dropped-term variants give $n^2/(n+1)$, $n(n+1)$ and $n^2$, none of which has 9 as a root, so 9 sits one below the key rather than at the end of a route.

question.full_text:
A tuning fork is used to produce resonance in a glass tube. The length of the air column in this tube can be adjusted by a variable piston. At room temperature of $27^\circ\mathrm{C}$ two successive resonances are produced at $20\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $73\,\mathrm{cm}$ of column length. If the frequency of the tuning fork is $320\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the velocity of sound in air at $27^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is
(1) $330\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(2) $350\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(3) $339\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(4) $300\,\mathrm{m/s}$
question.html:
A tuning fork is used to produce resonance in a glass tube. The length of the air column in this tube can be adjusted by a variable piston. At room temperature of 27°C two successive resonances are produced at 20 cm and 73 cm of column length. If the frequency of the tuning fork is 320 Hz, the velocity of sound in air at 27°C is
  1. (1)330 m/s
  2. (2)350 m/s
  3. (3)339 m/s
  4. (4)300 m/s
question.stem: A tuning fork is used to produce resonance in a glass tube. The length of the air column in this tube can be adjusted by a variable piston. At room temperature of $27^\circ\mathrm{C}$ two successive resonances are produced at $20\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $73\,\mathrm{cm}$ of column length. If the frequency of the tuning fork is $320\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the velocity of sound in air at $27^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is

solution.html:
1. v = 2 (ν) [L2 - L1]
  2. = 2 × 320 [73 - 20] × 10-2
  3. = 339.2 ms-1
  4. = 339 m/s
steps: $= 339\,\mathrm{m/s}$
Two successive resonance lengths in a resonance tube differ by half a wavelength: $l_2 - l_1 = \frac{\lambda}{2}$.
$\frac{\lambda}{2} = 73\,\mathrm{cm} - 20\,\mathrm{cm} = 53\,\mathrm{cm}$.
$\lambda = 2 \times 53\,\mathrm{cm} = 106\,\mathrm{cm} = 1.06\,\mathrm{m}$.
$v = f\lambda = 320\,\mathrm{Hz} \times 1.06\,\mathrm{m} = 339.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$339.2\,\mathrm{m/s} \approx 339\,\mathrm{m/s}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Two successive resonance lengths in a resonance tube differ by half a wavelength: l2 - l1 = λ2.
  2. λ2 = 73 cm - 20 cm = 53 cm.
  3. λ = 2 × 53 cm = 106 cm = 1.06 m.
  4. v = fλ = 320 Hz × 1.06 m = 339.2 m/s.
  5. 339.2 m/s ≈ 339 m/s, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Successive resonances differ by lambda/2, so lambda = 2(73 - 20) cm = 106 cm and v = 320 x 1.06 = 339.2 m/s, about 339 m/s.

solution.full_text:
1. For isolated capacitor $Q = \text{Constant}$
2. $F_{\mathrm{plate}} = \frac{Q^{2}}{2A\varepsilon_{0}}$
3. $F$ is Independent of the distance between plates.

  2. Fplate = Q22Aε0

$F_{\mathrm{plate}} = \frac{Q^{2}}{2A\varepsilon_{0}}$

steps: The capacitor is isolated, so its charge $Q$ stays constant as $d$ changes.
Field due to one plate at the other plate: $E_1 = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0 A}$.
Force on the other plate: $F = Q E_1 = \frac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0 A}$.
$F$ contains no $d$, so it is independent of the distance between the plates, which is option $1$.

question.full_text:
An electron falls from rest through a vertical distance $h$ in a uniform and vertically upward directed electric field $E$. The direction of electric field is now reversed, keeping its magnitude the same. A proton is allowed to fall from rest in it through the same vertical distance $h$. The time of fall of the electron, in comparison to the time of fall of the proton is
(1) Smaller
(2) 10 times greater
(3) 5 times greater
(4) Equal
question.html:
An electron falls from rest through a vertical distance h in a uniform and vertically upward directed electric field E. The direction of electric field is now reversed, keeping its magnitude the same. A proton is allowed to fall from rest in it through the same vertical distance h. The time of fall of the electron, in comparison to the time of fall of the proton is
  1. (1)Smaller
  2. (2)10 times greater
  3. (3)5 times greater
  4. (4)Equal
question.stem: An electron falls from rest through a vertical distance $h$ in a uniform and vertically upward directed electric field $E$. The direction of electric field is now reversed, keeping its magnitude the same. A proton is allowed to fall from rest in it through the same vertical distance $h$. The time of fall of the electron, in comparison to the time of fall of the proton is

solution.full_text:
1. $h = \frac{1}{2}\frac{eE}{m}t^{2}$
2. $\therefore\ t = \sqrt{\frac{2hm}{eE}}$
3. $\therefore\ t \propto \sqrt{m}$ as ‘$e$’ is same for electron and proton.
4. $\because$ Electron has smaller mass so it will take smaller time.
solution.html:
1. h = 12eEmt2
  2. ∴ t = 2hmeE
  3. ∴ t ∝ m as ‘e’ is same for electron and proton.
  4. ∵ Electron has smaller mass so it will take smaller time.
steps: $h = \frac{1}{2}\frac{eE}{m}t^{2}$
$\therefore\ t = \sqrt{\frac{2hm}{eE}}$
$\therefore\ t \propto \sqrt{m}$ as ‘$e$’ is same for electron and proton.
$\because$ Electron has smaller mass so it will take smaller time.
printed_lines: m  as ‘e’ is same for electron and
Electron has smaller mass so it will take

steps: With $\vec{E}$ upward, the force on the electron $-e\vec{E}$ points downward, so $a_e = \frac{eE}{m_e}$ downward.
With $\vec{E}$ reversed (downward), the force on the proton $e\vec{E}$ points downward, so $a_p = \frac{eE}{m_p}$ downward.
Falling from rest through $h$: $h = \frac{1}{2} a t^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{2hm}{eE}}$.
$\frac{t_e}{t_p} = \sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m_p}} < 1$ since $m_e \ll m_p$.
Including gravity, $a_e = g + \frac{eE}{m_e} > a_p = g + \frac{eE}{m_p}$, so still $t_e < t_p$: the electron's time is smaller, option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. With →E upward, the force on the electron -e→E points downward, so ae = eEme downward.
  2. With →E reversed (downward), the force on the proton e→E points downward, so ap = eEmp downward.
  3. Falling from rest through h: h = 12 a t2 ⇒ t = 2ha = 2hmeE.
  4. tetp = memp < 1 since me ≪ mp.
  5. Including gravity, ae = g + eEme > ap = g + eEmp, so still te < tp: the electron's time is smaller, option 1.
ai_solution.why: Both particles get the same electric force eE downward; acceleration eE/m is far larger for the lighter electron, so t = sqrt(2hm/(eE)) is smaller for the electron.

subtopics.name: Motion of Charged Particle in Uniform Electric Field
subtopics.why: The answer depends on the acceleration a = eE/m of a charged particle in a uniform field, so t = sqrt(2hm/eE) is smaller for the lighter electron.

step_list: Check force directions: upward field pushes the electron down, and the reversed (downward) field pushes the proton down, so both fall under a force of the same magnitude eE
Write the acceleration of each as a = eE/m, so the lighter electron accelerates far more than the proton
From h = (1/2)at^2, t = sqrt(2hm/eE), so t scales with sqrt(m); compare the two and conclude the electron's time is smaller (still true if gravity is added, since g is the same for both)
difficulty.why: Medium: three short, signposted steps with no arithmetic, but options 1 and 4 are both plausible. 'Equal' is what you get from the free-fall intuition or from seeing 'same field, same charge' and stopping there, and only writing a = eE/m separates the two. Options 2 and 3 ('10 times' and '5 times greater') match no mass ratio (sqrt(1836) is about 43) and have the trend the wrong way round, so they go on sight.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: A live 'Equal' rival reached by transferring the Galilean result (fall time does not depend on mass) from gravity to an electric field, helped by the stem's stress on equal field magnitude and equal distance. The field reversal also asks the candidate to check that both particles really do fall, which can distract from the mass comparison.

trap.label: condition_missed
trap.route: 'All bodies fall through the same height in the same time' is true because gravity gives every mass the same acceleration $g$; here the acceleration is $eE/m$, so the electron's much smaller mass makes it the faster faller and the times cannot be equal
trap.who: a student who imports the mass-independence of free fall, where $h = \frac12gt^2$ has no $m$ in it
trap.feels: the two particles carry equal charge magnitudes and fall through the same height $h$ in the same field magnitude, so everything in the problem looks symmetric

steps.text: Both particles start from rest and cover the same vertical distance $h$ under a constant force.
Time of fall does not depend on mass, so the two times are equal.
steps.fix: That rule holds only when the acceleration itself is mass-independent; here $a = eE/m$, so $t = \sqrt{2hm/eE}$ and the time scales as the square root of the mass.

other_options.proof: $t = \sqrt{2hm/eE}$ with $h$, $e$ and $E$ the same for both gives $t_e/t_p = \sqrt{m_e/m_p} = 1/43$, so the electron's time is smaller by a factor near 43. No ratio of the printed quantities produces 10, and the direction of this option is wrong as well as its size: nothing in the problem makes the electron slower.

The only numerical factor the problem contains is the mass ratio 1836 and its square root 43. 5 is neither, nor is it reachable from them by any single operation (the fourth root is 6.5, the logarithm is not a quantity the chapter uses), and like option 2 it also reverses which particle takes longer.

categories.note: asks is relation because the options are how-many-times answers about one quantity changing with another (the time with the mass), and no value is computed.

question.full_text:
A pendulum is hung from the roof of a sufficiently high building and is moving freely to and fro like a simple harmonic oscillator. The acceleration of the bob of the pendulum is $20\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ at a distance of $5\,\mathrm{m}$ from the mean position. The time period of oscillation is
(1) $2\pi\,\mathrm{s}$
(2) $2\,\mathrm{s}$
(3) $\pi\,\mathrm{s}$
(4) $1\,\mathrm{s}$
question.html:
A pendulum is hung from the roof of a sufficiently high building and is moving freely to and fro like a simple harmonic oscillator. The acceleration of the bob of the pendulum is 20 m/s2 at a distance of 5 m from the mean position. The time period of oscillation is
  1. (1)2π s
  2. (2)2 s
  3. (3)π s
  4. (4)1 s
question.stem: A pendulum is hung from the roof of a sufficiently high building and is moving freely to and fro like a simple harmonic oscillator. The acceleration of the bob of the pendulum is $20\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ at a distance of $5\,\mathrm{m}$ from the mean position. The time period of oscillation is

solution.full_text:
1. $|a| = \omega^{2}y$
2. $\Rightarrow\ 20 = \omega^{2}(5)$
3. $\Rightarrow\ \omega = 2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$
4. $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi\,\mathrm{s}$
solution.html:
1. |a| = ω2y
  2. ⇒ 20 = ω2(5)
  3. ⇒ ω = 2 rad/s
  4. T = 2πω = 2π2 = π s
steps: $|a| = \omega^{2}y$
$\Rightarrow\ 20 = \omega^{2}(5)$
$\Rightarrow\ \omega = 2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$
$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi\,\mathrm{s}$
In SHM the magnitude of acceleration is $|a| = \omega^2 x$.
$\omega^2 = \frac{a}{x} = \frac{20}{5} = 4\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$.
$\omega = 2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi\,\mathrm{s}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In SHM the magnitude of acceleration is |a| = ω2 x.
  2. ω2 = ax = 205 = 4 s-2.
  3. ω = 2 rad/s.
  4. T = 2πω = 2π2 = π s, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: In SHM |a| = omega^2 x, so omega^2 = 20/5 = 4, omega = 2 rad/s and T = 2pi/omega = pi s.

steps.text: $a = \omega^2x$ gives $\omega^2 = 20/5 = 4$, so $\omega = 2\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
The time period is therefore 2 s.
steps.fix: $\omega$ is in radians per second; convert with $T = 2\pi/\omega = \pi\,\mathrm{s}$.

other_options.proof: $2\pi\,\mathrm{s}$ needs $\omega = 1\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, i.e. $a/x = 1$; the printed 20 m/s squared and 5 m give $a/x = 4$, $x/a = 0.25$, $\sqrt{a/x} = 2$ and $\sqrt{x/a} = 0.5$, none of which is 1. Failing to take the square root gives $T = 2\pi/4 = \pi/2\,\mathrm{s}$, which is not printed either.

1 s needs $\omega = 2\pi\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, i.e. $a/x = 4\pi^2 \approx 39.5$, which the data do not give. It is also not any of the intermediate quantities ($\omega = 2$, $\omega^2 = 4$, $\sqrt{x/a} = 0.5$); reaching it needs $T = 2\sqrt{x/a}$, i.e. the whole factor $\pi$ dropped from the period formula.

question.full_text:
The power radiated by a black body is $P$ and it radiates maximum energy at wavelength, $\lambda_0$. If the temperature of the black body is now changed so that it radiates maximum energy at wavelength $\frac{3}{4}\lambda_0$, the power radiated by it becomes $nP$. The value of $n$ is
(1) $\frac{3}{4}$
(2) $\frac{256}{81}$
(3) $\frac{4}{3}$
(4) $\frac{81}{256}$
question.html:
The power radiated by a black body is P and it radiates maximum energy at wavelength, λ0. If the temperature of the black body is now changed so that it radiates maximum energy at wavelength 34λ0, the power radiated by it becomes nP. The value of n is
  1. (1)34
  2. (2)25681
  3. (3)43
  4. (4)81256
question.stem: The power radiated by a black body is $P$ and it radiates maximum energy at wavelength, $\lambda_0$. If the temperature of the black body is now changed so that it radiates maximum energy at wavelength $\frac{3}{4}\lambda_0$, the power radiated by it becomes $nP$. The value of $n$ is

solution.full_text:
1. We know, $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}\,T = \text{constant}$ (Wien's law)
2. So, $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}_1}T_1 = \lambda_{\mathrm{max}_2}T_2$
3. $\Rightarrow \lambda_0\,T = \frac{3\lambda_0}{4}T'$
4. $\Rightarrow T' = \frac{4}{3}T$
5. So, $\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^4 = \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^4 = \frac{256}{81}$
solution.html:
1. We know, λmax T = constant (Wien's law)
  2. So, λmax1T1 = λmax2T2
  3. ⇒ λ0 T = 3λ04T'
  4. ⇒ T' = 43T
  5. So, P2P1 = (T'T)4 = (43)4 = 25681
steps: We know, $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}\,T = \text{constant}$ (Wien's law)
So, $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}_1}T_1 = \lambda_{\mathrm{max}_2}T_2$
$\Rightarrow \lambda_0\,T = \frac{3\lambda_0}{4}T'$
$\Rightarrow T' = \frac{4}{3}T$
So, $\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^4 = \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^4 = \frac{256}{81}$
Wien's displacement law: $\lambda_m T = b$ (constant), so $T \propto \frac{1}{\lambda_m}$.
$\frac{T'}{T} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\frac{3}{4}\lambda_0} = \frac{4}{3}$.
Stefan-Boltzmann law: $P = \sigma A T^4$, so $P \propto T^4$ for the same body.
$n = \frac{P'}{P} = \left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^4 = \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^4 = \frac{256}{81}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Wien's displacement law: λm T = b (constant), so T ∝ 1λm.
  2. T'T = λ034λ0 = 43.
  3. Stefan-Boltzmann law: P = σ A T4, so P ∝ T4 for the same body.
  4. n = P'P = (T'T)4 = (43)4 = 25681, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Wien's law gives T' = (4/3)T when the peak wavelength becomes (3/4)lambda_0; Stefan's law P proportional to T^4 gives n = (4/3)^4 = 256/81.

chapter.name: Thermal Properties of Matter
chapter.why: The answer 256/81 depends on Wien's displacement law (T inversely proportional to lambda_max) combined with the Stefan-Boltzmann law (P proportional to T^4), which are the black-body radiation laws.

subtopics.name: Radiation Laws
subtopics.why: The answer 256/81 follows from Wien's displacement law (T inversely proportional to lambda_max, so T becomes 4T/3) combined with the Stefan-Boltzmann law (P proportional to T^4), both radiation laws.

step_list: Apply Wien's displacement law (lambda_max * T = constant): the peak moves from lambda_0 to (3/4)lambda_0, so the new temperature is T' = (4/3)T
Apply Stefan-Boltzmann for the same body (P proportional to T^4): n = (T'/T)^4 = (4/3)^4, evaluated as 4^4/3^4
difficulty.why: Medium: two short, standard steps (Wien then Stefan), and the options settle the exponent for you, since 1 and 3 are bare first-power ratios that anyone who remembers P proportional to T^4 drops on sight; but options 2 and 4 are reciprocals of each other, so the inverse relation in Wien's law still has to be applied correctly to choose between them.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The direction of the ratio: a shorter peak wavelength means a hotter body, and a candidate who carries the 3/4 through as if it were the temperature ratio lands exactly on option 4, the reciprocal of the right answer. The arithmetic is short (4^4 and 3^4) and is not a time sink.

trap.feels: the fourth power has plainly been applied, so the option looks like the product of the full method, and the stem's own fraction $3/4$ reappears in it

steps.text: Power goes as $T^4$, so $n = (T'/T)^4$.
The peak wavelength became $\frac34\lambda_0$, so $T' = \frac34T$ and $n = 81/256$.
steps.fix: Wien's law is $\lambda_mT = b$, an inverse relation: $T' = \frac43T$, so $n = (4/3)^4 = 256/81$.

other_options.who: a student who gets the Wien inversion right and reports the temperature ratio itself
other_options.feels: $4/3$ is the number the first law yields, and it is the only quantity in the working that the options seem to echo

steps.text: Wien's law gives $T' = \frac43T$.
So the power becomes $\frac43P$ and $n = 4/3$.
steps.fix: Stefan's law is still to be applied: $n = (4/3)^4 = 256/81$.

other_options.proof: $3/4$ is the wavelength ratio the stem prints, and reaching it as $n$ needs both the Wien inversion dropped and the fourth power dropped. Each single slip already has its own printed option: the dropped power lands on $4/3$ and the dropped inversion lands on $81/256$.

steps: Equal volumes give $A\,l_1 = 3A\,l_2$, so $l_2 = \frac{l_1}{3}$.

chapter.name: Mechanical Properties of Solids
chapter.why: The answer 9F follows from Young's modulus, F = YA(Δl)/l, applied to wires of equal volume (l2 = l1/3) and the same material, which is stress, strain and elasticity in Mechanical Properties of Solids.

subtopics.name: Determination of Young's Modulus
subtopics.why: The answer comes from the Young's modulus relation Y = FL/(A*Delta l) for wires of the same material; with equal volume L = V/A, so F is proportional to A^2 for equal extension, giving 9F.

step_list: Write Young's modulus relation Y = (F/A)/(dl/L), so the force for a given extension is F = Y A dl / L
Use equal volume (A L = 3A L2) to get the second wire's length L2 = L/3
Take the ratio F2/F1 = (A2/A1)(L1/L2) with the same Y and the same dl and read off the multiple of F
difficulty.why: Easy: three short steps that can all be done as a mental ratio, and the options carry no rival -- the one tempting wrong answer (3F, area ratio alone) is missing from the list, so a candidate who lands there is pushed straight back to the equal-volume step and none of the remaining distractors matches any slip.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The equal-volume constraint is the only non-trivial point: the length changes along with the area, so the factor is the square of the area ratio rather than the area ratio itself; a candidate who ignores it would fail, but the options do not reward that error.

source.note: Image shows '\u0394l' (Delta l) where the text layer draft had only 'l'; transcribed from the image. Typo 'socond' is printed in the source and kept as printed. Options are plain text (multiples of F), not drawings.

categories.concept: At fixed volume the length falls as the area rises, so $F = YA\Delta l/L$ scales as the square of the area

trap.route: Equal volume is read as 'nothing that matters has changed': since $AL$ is the same for both wires, the ratio $A/L$ is taken to be the same too, so the same force is thought to give the same extension - but $AL$ constant makes $A/L$ grow as $A^2$
trap.who: a student who notices the equal-volume condition and treats it as making the two wires equivalent rather than as fixing the second wire's length
trap.feels: the stem stresses that both wires are of the same material and the same volume, so the only printed difference seems to be cancelled by the volume condition

question.full_text:
A small sphere of radius $'r'$ falls from rest in a viscous liquid. As a result, heat is produced due to viscous force. The rate of production of heat when the sphere attains its terminal velocity, is proportional to
(1) $r^{3}$
(2) $r^{5}$
(3) $r^{2}$
(4) $r^{4}$
question.html:
A small sphere of radius 'r' falls from rest in a viscous liquid. As a result, heat is produced due to viscous force. The rate of production of heat when the sphere attains its terminal velocity, is proportional to
  1. (1)r3
  2. (2)r5
  3. (3)r2
  4. (4)r4
question.stem: A small sphere of radius $'r'$ falls from rest in a viscous liquid. As a result, heat is produced due to viscous force. The rate of production of heat when the sphere attains its terminal velocity, is proportional to

solution.full_text:
1. Power $= 6\pi\eta r V_{T} \cdot V_{T} = 6\pi\eta r V_{T}^{2}$
2. $V_{T} \propto r^{2}$
3. $\Rightarrow$ Power $\propto r^{5}$
solution.html:
1. Power = 6πη r VT · VT = 6πη r VT2
  2. VT ∝ r2
  3. ⇒ Power ∝ r5
steps: Power $= 6\pi\eta r V_{T} \cdot V_{T} = 6\pi\eta r V_{T}^{2}$
$V_{T} \propto r^{2}$
$\Rightarrow$ Power $\propto r^{5}$
At terminal velocity, $v_t = \frac{2 r^{2} (\rho - \sigma) g}{9 \eta}$, so $v_t \propto r^{2}$.
Viscous force by Stokes' law: $F = 6 \pi \eta r v_t \propto r \cdot r^{2} = r^{3}$.
Rate of heat production equals power against viscous force: $P = F v_t \propto r^{3} \cdot r^{2} = r^{5}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. At terminal velocity, vt = 2 r2 (ρ - σ) g9 η, so vt ∝ r2.
  2. Viscous force by Stokes' law: F = 6 π η r vt ∝ r · r2 = r3.
  3. Rate of heat production equals power against viscous force: P = F vt ∝ r3 · r2 = r5, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: At terminal velocity v is proportional to r^2, viscous force 6*pi*eta*r*v is proportional to r^3, so heat rate F*v is proportional to r^5.

If the volume of the steam produced is $167.1\,\mathrm{cc}$, the change in internal energy of the sample, is

solution.full_text:
1. $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$
2. $\Rightarrow\ 54 \times 4.18 = \Delta U + 1.013 \times 10^{5}(167.1 \times 10^{-6} - 0)$
3. $\Rightarrow\ \Delta U = 208.7\,\mathrm{J}$
solution.html:
1. Δ Q = Δ U + Δ W
  2. ⇒ 54 × 4.18 = Δ U + 1.013 × 105(167.1 × 10-6 - 0)
  3. ⇒ Δ U = 208.7 J
steps: $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$
$\Rightarrow\ 54 \times 4.18 = \Delta U + 1.013 \times 10^{5}(167.1 \times 10^{-6} - 0)$
$\Rightarrow\ \Delta U = 208.7\,\mathrm{J}$
First law of thermodynamics: $\Delta U = Q - W$, with $W = P\Delta V$ at constant pressure.
Heat supplied: $Q = 54\,\mathrm{cal} \times 4.18\,\mathrm{J\,cal^{-1}} \approx 225.7\,\mathrm{J}$.
Initial volume of $0.1\,\mathrm{g}$ water $= 0.1\,\mathrm{cc}$, so $\Delta V = 167.1 - 0.1 = 167.0\,\mathrm{cc} = 1.670 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3}$.
$W = P\Delta V = 1.013 \times 10^{5} \times 1.670 \times 10^{-4} \approx 16.9\,\mathrm{J}$.
$\Delta U = 225.7 - 16.9 \approx 208.8\,\mathrm{J}$, which matches $208.7\,\mathrm{J}$, option $3$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. Heat supplied: Q = 54 cal × 4.18 J cal-1 ≈ 225.7 J.
  3. Initial volume of 0.1 g water = 0.1 cc, so Δ V = 167.1 - 0.1 = 167.0 cc = 1.670 × 10-4 m3.
  4. W = PΔ V = 1.013 × 105 × 1.670 × 10-4 ≈ 16.9 J.
  5. Δ U = 225.7 - 16.9 ≈ 208.8 J, which matches 208.7 J, option 3.

subtopics.name: Heat, Internal Energy, and Work
subtopics.why: The answer comes from the first law, change in internal energy = heat supplied (54 cal) minus work done by the expanding steam (P x change in volume), which gives about 208.7 J.

step_list: Convert the heat supplied to joules: Q = 54 cal x ~4.2 J/cal, about 226 J
Work done by the expanding steam: W = P(V_steam - V_water) with volumes converted from cc to m^3 (167.1 - 0.1 = 167 cc = 1.67 x 10^-4 m^3), so W is about 1.013 x 10^5 x 1.67 x 10^-4, about 17 J
Apply the first law with the right sign: delta U = Q - W
difficulty.why: Easy: three short steps on a signposted first-law method, and the options settle it as soon as Q is in joules - W is plainly a small positive correction of about 17 J, so a candidate who knows delta U = Q - W only has to see which option is slightly under 226 J, and the usual slips (cc to m^3 done wrong, W added instead of subtracted, cal left unconverted) all land on values that are not options, so they get caught rather than rewarded.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The cc-to-m^3 conversion (10^-6) and the sign of the work term are the only traps, and both give answers that are not in the options; subtracting the 0.1 cc liquid volume is a detail that changes nothing at option precision.

trap.label: no_trap
trap.route: The routes that exist on these numbers are $Q = 54\times4.18 = 225.7\,\mathrm{J}$, $W = 1.013\times10^5\times167\times10^{-6} = 16.9\,\mathrm{J}$ and $\Delta U = 208.7\,\mathrm{J}$ (the key). Dropping the work gives 225.7 J and adding it instead of subtracting gives 242.6 J, and neither is printed; the three wrong options are 0.20, 0.40 and 0.50 of the key, and no operation on 54 cal, $1.013\times10^5\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ and 167.1 cc produces those factors.

other_options.proof: 104.3 J is exactly half the key, but the halving has to be applied to the answer, not to any input: halving the heat gives $112.9-16.9 = 96.0\,\mathrm{J}$ and halving the work gives $225.7-8.5 = 217.2\,\mathrm{J}$, neither of which is 104.3 J.

42.2 J requires the heat to be about 59 J, i.e. a calorie worth 1.09 J; the conversions in play are 4.18 and 4.2 J per calorie, giving 225.7 and 226.8 J. Working entirely in calories instead gives $54 - 4.05 = 49.95\,\mathrm{cal}$, which is not 42.2 in either unit.

84.5 J is twice 42.2 and needs the same unsupported factor. Checked the volume conversions as well: taking 167.1 cc as $167.1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}$ makes the work 16927 J and $\Delta U$ large and negative, and leaving the water's own 0.1 cc out of $\Delta V$ changes the work by only 0.01 J.

step_list: Convert the main scale reading 5 mm to 0.5 cm and find the circular scale contribution 25 x 0.001 cm = 0.025 cm
Add them to get the observed reading, 0.525 cm
Apply the zero-error correction with its sign: correct reading = observed reading - (zero error) = 0.525 - (-0.004) cm
difficulty.why: Hard on the options, not the arithmetic: three short steps, but three of the four options sit on the three possible treatments of the zero error (subtract it, add it, ignore it), so elimination does nothing and only applying the sign convention correctly separates them.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The sign convention for a negative zero error (correct = observed - zero error, so a negative error is added back) is the classic lost-sign trap, and the wrong-sign result and the uncorrected reading are both printed as options; the non-standard wording '25 divisions above the reference level' adds a moment of doubt about the circular scale reading.

source.note: No stacked fraction is visible in the crop despite the needs_image_read flag; the stem and options are plain text and match the text layer draft. Zero error is printed with a dash (–0.004 cm), transcribed as a minus sign.

categories.concept: A screw-gauge reading is main scale plus circular divisions times least count, and a negative zero error has to be added back, not taken off

trap.label: reversed

trap.who: a student who knows a zero error must be removed and removes it by subtracting its magnitude
trap.feels: 'correcting for an error' reads as taking something away, and the arithmetic is clean either way, so nothing in the number flags the sign

steps.text: Observed reading $= 5\,\mathrm{mm} + 25\times0.001\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.525\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Remove the zero error: $0.525 - 0.004 = 0.521\,\mathrm{cm}$.
steps.fix: Correct reading = observed reading minus zero error, and the zero error here is negative, so it is $0.525 + 0.004 = 0.529\,\mathrm{cm}$.

spec.title: Forces on a block resting on a wedge accelerating with a, including the pseudo force ma

steps: The figure shows the incline face rising to the left (from $B$ up to $A$), so its normal points up and to the right. Pushing the wedge to the right can therefore hold the block.
In the wedge frame, the block feels gravity $mg$ downward, a pseudo force $ma$ to the left, and the normal force $N$. The surface is smooth, so there is no friction.
Gravity's component down the slope (towards $B$) is $mg\sin\theta$.
The pseudo force's component up the slope (towards $A$) is $ma\cos\theta$.
For equilibrium along the incline: $ma\cos\theta = mg\sin\theta$.
$a = g\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = g\tan\theta$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The figure shows the incline face rising to the left (from B up to A), so its normal points up and to the right. Pushing the wedge to the right can therefore hold the block.
  2. In the wedge frame, the block feels gravity mg downward, a pseudo force ma to the left, and the normal force N. The surface is smooth, so there is no friction.
  3. Gravity's component down the slope (towards B) is mgsinθ.
  4. The pseudo force's component up the slope (towards A) is macosθ.
  5. For equilibrium along the incline: macosθ = mgsinθ.
  6. a = gsinθcosθ = gtanθ, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: In the wedge frame, the up-slope component of the pseudo force (ma cos theta) must balance the down-slope component of gravity (mg sin theta), giving a = g tan theta.

chapter.name: Laws of Motion
chapter.why: The answer a = g tan(theta) comes from applying Newton's second law to the block on an accelerating smooth wedge (N cos(theta) = mg, N sin(theta) = ma), which is a wedge/pseudo-force problem in Laws of Motion.

subtopics.name: Pseudo Force
subtopics.why: The answer a = g tan(theta) comes from balancing the pseudo force ma (in the accelerating wedge's frame) against gravity along the smooth incline, so ma cos(theta) = mg sin(theta).

step_list: Work in the wedge's frame: the block is at rest there, so add a pseudo force ma acting opposite to the wedge's acceleration (to the left), alongside mg and the normal reaction from the smooth face.

Resolve along the incline face (so the normal reaction drops out): set the up-slope component of the pseudo force equal to the down-slope component of gravity, then solve for a in terms of g and theta.
difficulty.why: Medium: two short steps (pseudo force in the wedge frame, then a balance along the incline), with one real rival. Option 1 is the free-slide acceleration in disguise, and a candidate who recalls 'smooth incline means g sin(theta)' instead of doing the balance lands on it. Options 2 and 3 fall away once any balance is written.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Option 1 is written as g/cosec(theta), so it has to be simplified before it shows up as the standard g sin(theta) result. The candidate must also see that the block is held in place by the normal reaction's horizontal push, not that it is sliding, so the fixed-incline formula is the wrong route even though it reaches option 1.

source.note: Stem figure (wedge ABC with block m, acceleration arrow a, angle theta at B) is inside the crop; figure_bbox given in crop pixels (crop is 729x698). Options 1 and 3 are stacked fractions (g over cosec theta, g over sin theta) read from the image; the text layer had collapsed them so options 1 and 3 looked identical.

categories.concept: In the wedge's frame the block is held by two resolved forces: $ma\cos\theta$ up the slope against $mg\sin\theta$ down it, giving $a = g\tan\theta$

trap.label: formula_misused
trap.route: The component of gravity along the slope, $mg\sin\theta$, is written down correctly and then set against the whole pseudo-force $ma$ rather than its component $ma\cos\theta$, which gives $a = g\sin\theta$ - the option printed as $g/\mathrm{cosec}\,\theta$
trap.who: a student who resolves the weight along the incline, as every static incline problem requires, and leaves the horizontal pseudo-force unresolved
trap.feels: $mg\sin\theta$ is the expression this geometry always starts from, and the option's unusual form $g/\mathrm{cosec}\,\theta$ hides that it is just $g\sin\theta$

steps.text: In the wedge's frame the block feels $mg$ down and a pseudo-force $ma$ backwards; along the slope gravity contributes $mg\sin\theta$.
Balance that against the pseudo-force: $ma = mg\sin\theta$, so $a = g\sin\theta = g/\mathrm{cosec}\,\theta$.
steps.fix: The pseudo-force is horizontal, so only $ma\cos\theta$ lies along the slope; $ma\cos\theta = mg\sin\theta$ gives $a = g\tan\theta$.

other_options.who: a student who resolves the weight perpendicular to the slope and balances the unresolved pseudo-force against that component
other_options.feels: $mg\cos\theta$ is the other component every incline problem writes down, and it is the one that appears in the normal reaction

steps.text: Set $ma = mg\cos\theta$, so $a = g\cos\theta$.
steps.fix: Resolve both forces along the same axis; taken along the slope they give $ma\cos\theta = mg\sin\theta$.

other_options.who: a student who resolves the pseudo-force but leaves the weight whole
other_options.feels: the pseudo-force is the new ingredient, so it is the one that gets the attention and the trigonometric factor, and $g/\sin\theta$ looks like the matching rearrangement

steps.text: Set $ma\sin\theta = mg$, so $a = g/\sin\theta$.
steps.fix: The same axis has to be used for both: along the slope the weight contributes $mg\sin\theta$ and the pseudo-force $ma\cos\theta$.

question.full_text:
A toy car with charge $q$ moves on a frictionless horizontal plane surface under the influence of a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$. Due to the force $q\vec{E}$, its velocity increases from $0$ to $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in one second duration. At that instant the direction of the field is reversed. The car continues to move for two more seconds under the influence of this field. The average velocity and the average speed of the toy car between $0$ to $3$ seconds are respectively
(1) $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(2) $1\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $3.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(3) $1\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(4) $1.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$

[Figure: Toy car path A to B and back to C with times, velocities and accelerations]
1. Acceleration $a = \frac{6-0}{1} = 6\,\mathrm{ms^{-2}}$
2. For $t = 0$ to $t = 1\,\mathrm{s}$,
3. $S_1 = \frac{1}{2}\times 6(1)^2 = 3\,\mathrm{m}$ ...(i)
